summary.text: Earth's magnetic field reaches from deep inside the planet out into space, where it meets the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun.
It is made by electric currents in churning molten iron and nickel in the outer core, stirred by heat escaping from the core in a process called a geodynamo.
The field shields Earth from charged particles that would otherwise strip away the upper atmosphere, including the ozone layer that blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation.

facts.label: Surface strength
facts.value: About 30,000 to 60,000 nT in a 2019 survey

facts.label: Strongest and weakest
facts.value: About 60,000 nT over Siberia, 30,000 nT over Brazil

facts.label: Pole swaps
facts.value: At irregular intervals averaging several hundred thousand years

facts.label: Animal navigators
facts.value: Some bacteria and pigeons use it to orient

items.prompt: The north end of a compass needle swings toward the Arctic. Since opposite magnetic poles attract, what kind of pole of Earth's own field must lie up there?

options.label: The south pole of Earth's field
The north pole of Earth's field
No pole, just flat field lines
A pole that switches every day

items.explain: A needle's north end is pulled toward an opposite pole, so the geomagnetic pole in the Arctic is really the south pole of Earth's field.

items.prompt: Calculations suggest Mars once lost its magnetic field while the solar wind kept scavenging ions from it. What happened to the planet's air?

options.label: It grew thicker over time
Almost all of it was lost
It froze onto the ground
Nothing changed at all

items.explain: Without a field to deflect the solar wind, ions were carried away, and the loss of the field led to a near total loss of the Martian atmosphere.

items.prompt: A friend says Earth is magnetic because its centre is one giant solid bar magnet. What actually produces the field?

options.label: Magnetized rocks in the crust
The solar wind charging the air
Currents in moving molten metal in the core
A frozen iron magnet at the centre

items.explain: The bar magnet is only an approximation; the field comes from electric currents in convecting molten iron and nickel in the outer core.

items.prompt: You carry a needle that shows the field's angle with the horizontal, walking from the North Magnetic Pole to the magnetic equator. How does the needle behave?

options.label: It stays level the whole way
It starts level and tilts down more
It points straight up the whole way
It starts straight down and slowly levels out

items.explain: The field points straight down at the North Magnetic Pole and rotates upward as latitude drops, until it is horizontal at the magnetic equator.

items.prompt: Rocks on the sea floor form stripes with alternating magnetic directions, centred on mid-ocean ridges where the floor is spreading. What do the stripes record?

options.label: Flips of the field as new sea floor formed
Lightning strikes on the ocean surface
Iron washed out to sea by rivers
The daily swing of tides over the ridge

items.explain: Igneous rock records the field's polarity, so reversals show up as stripes around ridges where sea floor is spreading.

items.prompt: A strong refrigerator magnet clings to a steel door. How does the strength of Earth's field at the surface compare with that magnet's field?

options.label: Earth's is about the same strength
Earth's is hundreds of times weaker
Earth's is hundreds of times stronger
Earth's is millions of times stronger

items.explain: Earth's field ranges from about 0.30 G to 0.60 G, while a strong refrigerator magnet has about 100 G, hundreds of times more.

pack.question: Where does Earth's magnetic field come from, and what does it do for us?

beats.title: A Magnet Made of Molten Metal
beats.hook: Every compass needle is being steered by molten metal churning deep inside the planet.

beats.prompt: A planet's magnetic field dies out, but the Sun keeps blasting it with charged particles. What happens to its atmosphere over time?
beats.explain: Without a field, the solar wind's charged particles strip away the atmosphere; calculations for Mars show losing its field led to a near total loss of its air.

choices.label: It freezes into a solid shell
choices.feedback: Nothing here involves freezing; the loss comes from the solar wind carrying gas away.

choices.label: It grows thicker as particles pile up
choices.feedback: The particles do not collect; they scavenge gas and carry it off.

choices.label: Nothing, since fields have no effect on gas
choices.feedback: The field matters because it deflects the charged solar wind that would strip the air.

choices.label: Most of it gets stripped away

beats.prompt: Match each way of describing the field to what it measures

right.label: Angle the field makes with the horizontal
Heat-driven churning that creates the field
Angle between magnetic north and true north
Proportional to the force on a magnet

beats.explain: Direction is described by two angles, declination and inclination, strength by intensity, and the geodynamo is the process that makes the field in the first place.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Heat escaping the core stirs molten iron and nickel.
The moving metal carries electric currents that create the field.
So the magnetic poles stay fixed in one place forever.
Compasses still work for navigation because the poles drift slowly.

beats.explain: The poles move slowly and continuously, and at irregular intervals the field even reverses so the poles switch places.

beats.prompt: Sort each into where it happens

left.label: Convection of molten iron and nickel

beats.explain: The field is generated by convection in the outer core, then reaches out into space, where its extent forms the magnetosphere and it meets the solar wind.

beats.idea: Heat escaping the core stirs molten iron and nickel into currents that make a field, which deflects the solar wind and keeps the atmosphere from being stripped away.
